name: Bilal Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing accounting and finance. My week has two lectures on financial reporting, a spreadsheet lab, and a business law class I didn't expect to like. I rent a room in a flat on Dunmore Road, and my mum, who's a dentist, and my dad, who's a civil engineer, pay for it all. I play five-a-side football on Tuesdays and sometimes use an AI tool to explain a spreadsheet formula when I'm stuck at night.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because it's steady, and my uncle Karim does audits and says there's always work. My results were average, so I didn't aim for something flashy. Now I keep reading that accounting is high on the list for AI, which is slightly annoying after choosing it for safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that makes my choice look sensible. I'd tell friends the hype is cooling and that a lot of firms are going back to normal hiring. I wouldn't post anything, but I'd text my uncle Karim to say I'd stay on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means accounting stays a decent career, with routine tasks like data entry and reconciliations made a bit faster. I'd still need to do well in my first year to get on a graduate scheme. Average marks means I'm not the top choice for the big four, so I'd aim at mid-size firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up with my reports and labs, and aim for a placement with a local firm next summer. I'd start the professional exams as soon as I'm allowed, because they set me apart. And I'd learn spreadsheet and basic coding skills a bit at a time, through short online courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. I'd feel that I picked well, but I still have to earn the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does earning the job look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grades that aren't embarrassing, a placement, and being someone partners want to keep. My uncle says firms hire people they can stand for ten hours in an office, so being easy to work with counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else weighing on you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the cost of living in a big city. I'm fine because my parents pay, but I know my sister Nadia will start next year, and that doubles the costs for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is real and accounting is right in the middle of it. Checking, planning and booking are what junior accountants do. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now and get the professional qualification, because people still need someone to sign things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the entry-level jobs thin out first, and my average results make that worse. The big firms may hire fewer graduates and expect the rest to do more with software. By the time I graduate in three years, the grad scheme I'm aiming at could be half the size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more, not just for formulas but to practise checking a ledger. I'd go for the professional exams early, since those still need a person's name. I'd also talk to Uncle Karim about which firms are hiring and what skills they now ask for, and I'd try for work in advisory, which depends more on talking with clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. My career feels like a ladder with the bottom rungs being sawn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know if it was getting worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the placements for next year start shrinking, or if the firms start asking for coding on top of accounting. That's the sign for me to add skills, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend in the same course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the exams, learn the tools, and talk to someone in the industry now. If you wait until the final year, the choices are already made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the end of accounting as we know it, and that governments and firms need to talk now. Two years is nothing. I'd tell my family to prepare, because money and jobs will shift before anyone is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I chose the one degree that disappears first. Accounting is almost all thinking work. By 2028 I'd be in my second year, and the entry-level jobs would be done by software. I'd also worry about my parents, since dentistry is hands-on and safe until 2031, but my dad's engineering is partly design work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about what I should study that's closer to the physical world. I'd look at whether I can switch into something like construction management or finance with a hands-on side. I'd also ask them to keep their savings safe. And I'd cut my costs and stop buying stuff for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a knot in my stomach. I'd probably go quiet around my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really switch course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into it, definitely. It's embarrassing, because I just started, but I'd rather change in my first or second year than finish something that has no jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel that the notice is only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like there's no space to do it properly. A decade lets you plan; two years lets you only react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window. Firms will hire fewer juniors, but not zero. I'd tell friends to get the qualification and stay flexible. I'd say people should try to be useful in ways the machines aren't, like talking to clients and making judgement calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not scared. By 2031 I'd be about 23 and finishing the first years of a job. The risk is that graduate schemes shrink before I get in. The safeguard is that I'd have had time to prepare, which two years doesn't give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with solid marks, do the professional exams in parallel, and use my summers for placements. I'd use AI at a deeper level, like building small tools to check data. And I'd keep an eye on adjacent jobs: tax advice, advisory, or working with small business owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Five years of this feels like a long exam period. Not fun, but I know when the paper is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing, since my parents cover me. But I'd stop treating that as permanent. I'd keep a small buffer from any summer job so I'm not leaning on them after I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five-year gap change what you'd tell your sister Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to try accounting if she likes it, but to treat tools as part of the course. And I'd say to talk to people two years ahead of her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we'll sort out a lot of it as we go. I'd tell friends to work for a while, build skills, and not assume anything. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 28, qualified and probably working for a few years. Whatever the job looks like then, I'll have adapted. I'd feel more for the people who are 50 now and have less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, a placement and the exams, then spend my twenties picking up whatever the work needs. I'd save in my first few jobs, since I'd have a buffer for a gap or a move. I'd also keep an eye on the news about rules and regulations, because accounting depends on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade makes it a normal career challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm OK, I've planned, and they don't need to worry. Mum worries about everything, so I'd bring her a spreadsheet to prove it. My mum believes numbers more than reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A spreadsheet of what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, qualifications timeline, which firms I'd apply to. It's ridiculous, but she believes numbers more than reassurance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Accounting is all thinking work, and two years is too short to change course properly. What would help is firms and universities being honest about which entry jobs will remain, and a support scheme for graduates who can't find work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I picked accounting for safety, and the interview made me realise safety is not a fixed thing. I'd like someone to explain how people like me can plan when the target keeps moving.

headlineQuote: A decade lets you plan; two years lets you only react.
portrait: Bilal is an 18-year-old **accounting** student whose parents, a dentist and a civil engineer, cover rent and fees.
He chose accounting for safety, uses AI tools now and then, and plans carefully with **exams** and placements.
He is centrist and practical, leaning on his uncle Karim for **advice** and on spreadsheets to calm his mother.
His mood runs from uneasy in the plateau to **anxious** in the faster worlds, because accounting is almost all thinking work.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries him most, because accounting is thinking work and two years is too short to change course.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information** from firms and universities about which entry jobs remain, plus support for graduates who can't find work.
